demuestran asi que estan mejor preparadas para el ataque a la bayoneta 
(peones), sobre la ciudadela adversaria, tematica primordial para este 
tipo de posiciones)} 17...f6 18.h4 f5 19.Rdg1 Bb5 20.gxf5 Bxd3 21.Qxd3 
Rxf5 22.Be3 $1 {(El conductor de las negras ha procurado bloquear el 
ataque que se cernia sobre su enroque. Sin embargo, su estrategia se 
quiebra luego de este movimiento de las blancas, que lleva una doble 
funcion: apuntalar el peon en "f4" y dejar libre la casilla "d4" para que 
el caballo quiebre el bloqueo, al provocar el obligado retiro de la torre 
negra)} 22...Qc8 23.Nd4 Rf7 24.Rg6 $16 {(Las negras se han preparado para 
anular el rompimiento por la casilla "f4", pero no pueden controlar todas 
sus debilidades, ni la aguda filtracion de las figuras enemigas)} 24...Qc4
{(Se busca desgastar material (cambio de piezas) para aliviar la tension, 
pero igualmente todo se desmorona)} 25.Nxe6 Qxd3 26.cxd3 Rc8 27.Rhg1 {(Las
blancas rubrican una limpia faena)} 27...Bxh4 28.Rxh6 Be7 29.Rh5 {
Comentarista: Franco Luis Di Luca (h)} 1-0

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.c3 dxc3 {Of course the Goring Gambit may be 
declined in a number of days e.g. 4...d5, 4...d6 ora 4...Nf6; the last 
being a strong but underestimated counter to White's gambit. According to 
Penrose declining the gambit with 4...d5 is overestimated and a game of 
mine vs Homaka played in round 6 of the Olympiad illustrated Black's 
problems after 4...d5 5. exd5 Qxd5 etc.} 5.Nxc3 {To avoid the highly 
dubious line into which wWhite is now forced 5. Bc4 should be played. 
Bearing this in mind and considering that my last round opponent, Gomes 
might have prepared for the variation I played this against him and after 
the superlfuous defensive move 5...h6? proceeded to annihilate my opponent
6. Nxc3 d6 7. Qb3 Qd7 8. Qc2! etc.} 
    ( 5.Bc4 {The strength of this move may be shown by the following 
    plausible variation} 5...cxb2 6.Bxb2 Bb4+ 7.Nc3 Nf6 8.Qc2 d6 9.O-O-O 
    O-O 10.e5 Ng4 11.Nd5 Bc5 12.exd6 cxd6 13.h4 h6 14.Ng5 hxg5 15.hxg5 
    Qxg5+ 16.f4 Bf5 17.fxg5 Bxc2 18.Kxc2 {and although two pawns down 
    White has a tremendous attack and it is doubtful whether Black can 
    muster a defence.} )
5...Bb4 6.Bc4 Bxc3+ 7.bxc3 d6 8.O-O Nf6 9.e5 $1 {An improvement on 9. Ba3 
Bg4! which was found wanting in Penrose-Smyslov Munich 1958.} 9...Nxe5 $1 
    ( 9...dxe5 10.Qb3 $1 O-O 11.Rd1 {White has more than adequate 
    compensation for the two sacrified pawns.} )
10.Nxe5 dxe5 11.Qb3 Qe7 12.Ba3 c5 13.Bb5+ {An improvement.} 
    ( 13.Qb5+ Nd7 {Penrose-Unzicker, Leipzig 1960} )
13...Kf8 $1 {Although after the game Donner indicated that he thought this
was dubious it is in fact the only real attempt for Black to win as after 
this move, although somewhat undeveloped Black has a rock-solid position 
which is difficult to penetrate, and for his inconvenience is two good 
pawns up. The position now is critical for the variation and although 
Velimirovis favours White it is very doubtful whether White's active 
position is adequate compensation for the two pawn deficit.} 
    ( 13...Bd7 {Donner} 14.Bxd7+ Nxd7 15.Qxb7 O-O 16.Rad1 {Black has no 
    winning chances whatsoever} 16...Rfd8 17.Bxc5 Qxc5 18.Rxd7 Rxd7 19.
    Qxa8+ Qf8 $10 )
14.f4 $1 {The only active continuation.} 14...e4 
    ( 14...Be6 {may be even stronger, e.g.} 15.c4 $5 exf4 16.Rxf4 a6 17.
    Ba4 b5 18.Qe3 b4 19.Bb2 $13 )
15.f5 {Cramping Black, however the now succeeds, at some cost to his 
clock, to unravel his position and develop his game in what is probably 
the best possible way.} 15...h6 $1 
    ( 15...h5 $6 {Is worse; Smederevac-Minic.} )
16.Rae1 Kg8 17.c4 
    ( 17.Bc4 $5 )
17...Kh7 18.Qe3 b6 19.Bb2 
    ( 19.Bc6 {White could have regained one of his sacrificed pawns here; 
    e.g.} 19...Bb7 20.Bxb7 Qxb7 21.Bb2 Qe7 $1 
        ( 21...Rae8 22.Bxf6 gxf6 23.Rf4 )
    22.Bxf6 Qxf6 23.Qxe4 {but his temporary initiative and weakened pawn 
    structure do not compensate for the pawn deficit; in any event the 
    spirit of the gambit is not to fight for draw an inferior endgame!} )
19...Bb7 20.h3 $1 {Continuing the logical plan of bringing his pieces to 
bear on Black's king position and preparing a pawn storm, White has also 
attempted to maximize his attacking chances.} 20...Rad8 21.Ba4 Rd6 
    ( 21...Qd6 22.Rd1 Qe7 23.g4 Rxd1 24.Bxd1 {and White is not without 
    chances.} )
22.g4 Rhd8 {Both sides have developed logically but Black's good defensive
plan has cost him 2 hours on the clock thus leaving him 30 minutes for his
remaining 18 moves (White has used 1h15m).} 23.g5 hxg5 {Played 
automatically but 23...Nh5 might have been better.} 
    ( 23...Nh5 $5 24.f6 $1 gxf6 25.Bd1 $1 {with complications probably not
    unfavourable to Black.} )
24.Qxg5 Rd3 $2 {Amazingly enough to slip that costs Black the game. If 
Black had played 24...Rd2! which was the logical complement of his 
previous play this would have merely confirmed the dubious nature of 
White's move order i.e. 5. Nxc3 instead of 5. Bc4 and gives the game some 
theoretical importance as to my knowledge this is the first game in which 
Black has constructed the best possible defensive configuration i.e. h6, 
Kf8, Kg8, Kh7, b6, Bb7, Rad8, Rd6 and Rhd8.} 
    ( 24...Rd2 $1 {would have caused White serious problems, e.g.} 25.Rf2 
        ( 25.Bxf6 Qxf6 {and White has nothing.} )
        ( 25.Bc1 e3 $1 26.Bxd2 Rxd2 27.Qh4+ 
            ( 27.Rxe3 Qxe3+ $1 28.Qxe3 Rg2+ 29.Kh1 Rg3+ 30.Kh2 Rxe3 $19 )
        27...Kg8 28.Rf4 Rg2+ 29.Kf1 e2+ 30.Rxe2 Qxe2# )
    25...Rxf2 26.Kxf2 e3+ 
        ( {or} 26...Qd6 )
    27.Qxe3 Ne4+ {and White has extreme defensive problems.} )
25.Rf4 R8d4 
    ( 25...Rxh3 26.Rh4+ Rxh4 27.Qxh4+ Kg8 28.Re3 $1 {and the threat of Rh3
    cannot be parried[%draw full,e3,red][%draw arrow,e3,h3,red]} )
26.Bxd4 cxd4 27.Rh4+ Kg8 28.Rg4 $1 g6 29.fxg6 Qd6 30.gxf7+ Kxf7 31.Qg6+ 
Ke7 
    ( 31...Ke6 32.Rgxe4+ $1 )
32.Qg7+ Ke6 
    ( 32...Kd8 33.Qh8+ )
33.Rg6 Rf3 
    ( 33...Qe5 34.Qd7# )
    ( 33...Qe7 34.Qxe7+ Kxe7 35.Rg7+ $18 )
34.Qg8+ Kf5 35.Rg5+ Kf4 36.Rg4+ Ke5 
    ( 36...Nxg4 37.Qxg4+ Ke5 38.Qxf3 $18 )
37.Rg5+ Kf4 38.Qg6 Bc8 39.Qh6 Rxh3 40.Rf1+ $1 Ke3 41.Rg3+ {With Bd1 mate 
on the next move. An interesting although not faultless game. Black's 
defence after move 29 was very tenacious considering he had only 4 minutes
left on the clock to make his moves to the time control, also a 
theoretically important game and from now on I'll play 5. Bc4! instead of 
5. Nxc3 as after 13...Kf8! I'm sure Black is winning regardless of the 
game's result.} 1-0

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bg5 h6 5.Bh4 c5 6.d5 b5 {(La jugada en 
gambito que reexhumo Tal ante Spassky en el torneo de Tallin de 1973, con 
muy buen resultado. La idea consiste en "volar" el centro blanco para 
poder contragolpear alli con los peones negros. En la Olimpiada de Niza 
del ano 1974, Adamski aplico ante Cooper el mismo estudio, pero una vez 
mas se confirmo la vieja sentencia de que toda la gloria del mundo es 
pasajera: los profundos analisis que se habian realizado sobre la 
tematica, permitireron a las blancas acceder a un brillante triunfo. 
Unzicker tambien trabajo la idea y la empleo ante Spassky muy poco despues
que lo hiciese Tal, es decir en Bath del ano 1973)} 7.dxe6 fxe6 8.cxb5 d5 
9.e3 O-O 10.Bd3 
    ( {La primera mejora aplicada a la partida Spassky-Tal que habia 
    proseguido:} 10.Nf3 Qa5 11.Bxf6 Rxf6 12.Qd2 a6 13.bxa6 Nc6 {(Di Luca)}
    14.Be2 d4 15.exd4 Rxf3 16.Bxf3 cxd4 17.O-O dxc3 18.bxc3 Bxc3 19.Qd6 
    Rxa6 20.Bxc6 Bb4 21.Qb8 Rxc6 22.Rac1 Bc5 23.Rc2 Qa4 24.Qb3 Qf4 25.Qg3 
    Qf5 26.Rfc1 Bb7 27.Qf3 Qg5 28.Qb3 Rc7 29.g3 Bxf2+ 30.Kxf2 Qf6+ 31.Ke1 
    Qe5+ 32.Kf1 Ba6+ 33.Kg1 Qd4+ 34.Kg2 Qe4+ 35.Kg1 Bb7 36.h4 Qh1+ 37.Kf2 
    Rf7+ 38.Ke2 Qe4+ {0-1; Spassky-Tal; Tallin, 1973} )
10...d4 11.exd4 cxd4 12.a3 Ba5 13.b4 dxc3 14.bxa5 Bb7 15.Ne2 
    ( {Aqui la novedad probada en la partida Cooper-Adamski. Lo conocido 
    era:} 15.Nf3 Qxa5 16.O-O Nbd7 17.Qe2 Bxf3 18.Qxf3 Ne5 $15 {(Di Luca)} 
    19.Qe2 Nxd3 20.Qxd3 Nd5 21.Bg3 Rac8 22.Be5 Rf7 23.Rfe1 Qb6 24.Re2 Qc5 
    {1/2-1/2; Spassky-Unzicker; Bath, 1973} )
15...Qxa5 
    ( {Asi Unzicker se desvia de lo ocurrido en la partida Cooper-Adamski,
    la cual siguio:} 15...Bxg2 16.Rg1 Bf3 17.Bc2 Nbd7 18.Qd6 Bxe2 19.Kxe2
